utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon. How do we know that we are connected to our witness? There we go. Thank you very much. May the witness please -- I beg your pardon. I just wanted to remind the witness that you did take a declaration yesterday, ma'am, or made a declaration yesterday, to tell the truth the whole truth and nothing else but the truth. I remind you that you're still bound by that declaration to tell the truth today. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, ma'am. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam. Can you see me and can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to return to that Washington Post article by Joseph Nye. The version we had yesterday is in as Exhibit 1024. I wanted to remind you what you said yesterday about that article. You said twice that you had the article in front of you when you wrote the report. You said that you had the actual newspaper. You told us that the quotation -- Madam, you told us that the quotation in your report from -- the quotation in your report at page 4, that, "Secession is not a legal category or a rule of international law," is contained in the actual newspaper, and finally you told us that you had read the newspaper in its English version. Now, over night, and thanks from our side goes to our intern, Ms. Walker, we have obtained the original newspaper. It's in e-court now as 06051083 and the Registrar, there, has a copy of it as well. And there are two pages, the first page shows just the article and the second page shows the article on the page, and you can see that it's from the Washington Post, December 15th, 1992. It's the article by Joseph Nye called "the self-determination trap". The entire article is contained on that one page. Now, Madam, I'm not going to ask you to read through the entire article. I've checked it. It is identical to the version that we put into evidence yesterday, and it does not contain the quotation that you attribute to the article, that is, "secession is not a legal category or a rule of international law." That is not contained in this article. Can you explain how it's possible that that error is in your report?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There must have been a mistake that occurred, but I was unable to find that part today, but therefore it is possible. I would like to say one other thing. I don't understand why you keep insisting on this point when, before that bit, I quoted the position by U thant and that of the United Nations. While I suppose then that the United Nations' view must be the most relevant one when discussing this subject matter. That is why I consider all the extra discussion quite unnecessary and superfluous.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if you perhaps wish to challenge U thant's position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm focused now still on this article by Joseph Nye. You also say in -- about this article, you say that he severely criticises Clinton administration's "policies of new tribalism". Now, the quotation, "policies of new tribalism" also does not appear in the article. There is a reference to new tribalism and there is also no criticism of the Clinton administration policies in the article. It is simply recommending to the Clinton administration what approach it might take. Can you explain for us how, if you had this article in front of you when you were writing the report, how all of these errors could have been made? How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are going overboard, sir. This was just one single mistake, and not a fundamental one at that. And it is quite possible that -- please allow me to finish -- in this book of mine which was published in 19 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, please stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, could you answer my question? How is it possible? You told us yesterday at the beginning of cross-examination that your work ethic is to be precise and careful in your work. How is it possible that in so many respects, you could describe this article incorrectly in your report?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this book, I used not just this one article by Mr. Nye but also many other writings of his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has been translated and it is quite possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please stop. We've got to finish with you and go to the next witness. So please try to answer the question that's put to you. You are not being asked a question about your book, you are being asked a question about mistakes in this article. Try to answer that question and don't tell us about your book.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely what I'm trying to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't talk about your book, then, talk about the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And to approach that issue, really, smoothly, Mr. Whiting, you said you organised to have the whole issue of Washington Post of December 15th of this year, or 1992, and so you -- this is just a clip from, well, from which page, from which -- can we establish if this is part of that edition, of that issue? And then if, yes, is that the only page which was now found in this hurry? Was there anything on page 1 or on this page, as we discussed it might have been part of a dossier on several pages? Did you check that and can we see that? Can we see the whole newspaper? We have only one clip here now, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But Mr. Whiting said the whole article is on one page in this newspaper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Which page is it, and of which newspaper, and so and so on. I mean, this is just a paper clip. It's not a reliable --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please do it as thoroughly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe I did it too quickly, but at the beginning I indicated that on the second page of the exhibit, it says, Washington Post, it indicates that it's the Washington Post Tuesday, December 15th, 1992. The page number is a little hard to read, but it appears to be A22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I confess I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Here it is on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's the second page of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, now I see it. So it is a fax copy of a whole newspaper page then?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. We did not get the -- we could not, in that short time get the entire newspaper. We got this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No, I can establish that is was the Washington Post of Tuesday, December 15, 199 -- probably 2, A22.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This is what I read here, and this is number L6051084.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Whiting, having regard to what Judge Hoepfel had said we should get on the record the fact that the article appears to be in its entirety on that page and there is no semblance of continuation on any other page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: She has, by her answers, accepted that that is the article itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. And it's, of course, my intention also to put the article into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, I'll just put the question one last time. And if you don't have an answer for it, then just we can leave the issue. Are you able to explain for us, given that you told us you had this article in front of you when you wrote the report, the report was written just some months ago, I believe, how is it that you could make so many mistakes in describing the article? How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the article at the time when I was writing this book, and I quoted it on page 155, and the precise definition or reference was A23. And it was from this book that I took this article. The book was published and you have it at the Tribunal. It was published back in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this book, therefore, can be found at the Tribunal's premises, and you can also see from where it was taken. Now, as for the errors in quoting, well, I can't account for that. But at any rate the reference in my book is A23.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Madam --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I worked abroad and wrote the book there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The reference to A23 is your reference. That's what you put in the book, correct?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you would agree, would you not, that this is the article that you're talking about. It's the same article, even though it appears on A22? It is this article you're talking about in your report, not some other article; correct?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to examine the paper more thoroughly and I can't do that on the basis of this photocopy. At any rate, in my view, these four lines are not material for the main subject on which I drafted my expertise. It is an error, but it is not relevant, and it has no bearing whatsoever on my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Madam, I just want to get clear on one thing because yesterday, on two occasions, it's at 11098 and 11101, you told us that you had the actual article when you wrote the report. Are you now saying that, in fact, you did not have the article, but you had the book and that you relied on the book?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: I did have the article, yes, at the time I was writing this book. And this particular reference comes from the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why, then, did you tell us yesterday in your testimony on two occasions that you had the article when you were writing the report? Why did that happen?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm stating today that I had the article at one time. This is what I'm saying today as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used it for this book, as well as many other articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you're changing your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not, sir. I'm telling you again that I had the newspaper before me when I was writing this and quoting this. However, this took place when I was writing the book and then I took it -- I copied it from the book at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Well the transcript will speak for itself on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could these two pages be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which two pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The actual article that -- the two pages of the actual article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it two pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. May the newspaper cutting, whatever it is, the two pages of the newspaper be given an exhibit number? They are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 1026.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Madam, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Perovic? Just a second, ma'am, just a second, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to say something if you'll allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Perovic it is your turn to re- examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Madam.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, during cross-examination by my learned friend from the Prosecution, several questions from put to you concerning some constitutional provisions, and I mean the 1974 SFRY constitution.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: There was mention of Article 3 of the constitution, as well as Article 5 of the SFRY constitution from 1974. In Article 3 of the SFRY constitution, states are mentioned as the then socialist republics of the then SFRY. However, in Article 5 of the constitution, territorial integrity and inviolability of borders are guaranteed. Hence my question: Which borders are being referred to in Article 5 of the SFRY constitution? Which borders were the subject of protection of this constitution?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: International borders, as determined in international treaties after World War II, and annexes to the treaties concluded post-World War II in 1947. All the international treaties concluded or stipulated after World War I were ratified after World War II, since the allies were the same. There were only additional treaties for the parts where the borders of the post-World War II Yugoslavia changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Article 5 of the SFRY constitution serves to safeguard the borders of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can you please pause after -- Mr. Perovic, can you please pause after a long answer because that takes a long time then also to be translated. Thank you, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Hoepfel. I will bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Madam Avramov, the internal borders, that is the borders of federal units, based on what you've just told us, were not internationally recognised borders. These were not inter-state borders; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. These were administrative borders which did not even have an internal enactment delineating them. These borders -- INTERPRETER: There was a break in the videolink, the interpreter notes.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because every republic had its central party bodies as well as regional party bodies. These internal borders coincided with party borders. They have no significance whatsoever compared to international borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it, therefore, fair to say that Article 3 of the 1974 SFRY constitution made a concession for political reasons to the leaderships of individual republics when federal units were termed as states?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That question, as were the previous several questions, is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it is an absurd position that I should be able to suggest anything to the expert because she presented all her findings in her report, and in her oral evidence before the Trial Chamber. I'm quite certain of the fact that I cannot lead her in any way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why do you ask your questions, Mr. Perovic, why do you make statements to her and ask her to confirm them? Surely, and in any case, if you said everything is in evidence why are you re-examining her? I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I must confess, Mr. Whiting, my recollection is that an expert could be asked a leading question within the context of his expertise, because by the very nature of his expertise, he could be led and directed to the particular theoretical or philosophical statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: If there is jurisprudence to the contrary or practice as evidence of law to the contrary, then it's only a recollection of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm unable to cite to any jurisprudence or even practice on this issue except for my own jurisdiction where one would not be able to lead on, certainly not on conclusions from an expert. Perhaps there is more latitude for leading to get the expert to a certain point, but it seems to me these are asking for conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: From the perspective of a conclusion on particular points which are in issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: -- there should not be leading, you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That would be our position, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I would think the question could be allowed. Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Nosworthy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Madam Avramov, my question was: Was the term used in Article 3 of the 1974 SFRY constitution whereby federal units are defined as states within the SFRY an ideological concession or a concession for ideological reasons to the republics that then formed the SFRY? Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This article is a combination of -- yes, you're quite right -- of ideological views of the matter. Look at the second part of the article which speaks of the rule of the working people, which harks back to internationalism to a wider broader community which does not just end there. And this was a sort of copy of the Soviet model. But let me remind you that in international practice, federal units are termed differently. Whilst in Germany they are landen, whilst in Canada they are provinces, while in the United States they are states, and we know that the only state there is the United States of America under international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In connection with this issue, Madam Avramov, can Article 5 of the SFRY constitution guaranteeing territorial integrity of the SFRY be seen as derogating from Article 3 of the same constitution?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, in any -- never during any enactment or any public address of the leadership of the SFRY been the issue of territorial integrity of the SFRY called into question. And all the other enactments that were passed were passed from the point of view of Yugoslavia as a single state, and they all pointed to that direction. Therefore, there was supremacy of federal laws in relation to republican laws, and the same went for the federal courts and the republican judiciaries. There was nothing dubious or anything that would call into question the fact that the only state there was SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of yesterday's cross-examination, there was mention of the opinion of the so-called Badinter Commission, several questions were put to you on that subject. At the time which we've been discussing, not - - or not even nowadays, Yugoslavia is not a member or has never been a member of the European Union; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In light of that fact, from the perspective of international law, what sort of significance did the conclusion of the Badinter Commission have for the fate of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Badinter was presented as the future arbiter in this matter, the Serbian delegation lodged a protest in the course of the negotiations, challenging the legitimacy of this commission, because this had not been envisaged in the Brioni declaration, particularly not an attempt for the Badinter Commission to be taken as some kind of a judicial settlement of the problem, or the whole issue, and for this arbitration, this decision to be on the merits of the case. And we challenged the right of Badinter to even discuss this whole issue at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: So there is ample -- this has been amply documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In this regard, and in light of the fact that Yugoslavia was not a member of the European Union, would the opinion of the Badinter Commission have -- be binding for the then Yugoslavia, in your view as an expert?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, we strenuously objected to that and we did not accept it, we as the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, in the cross-examination yesterday, the UN Charter was mentioned. You presented your view that Article 1, paragraph 2, of the Charter, and many other provisions of this charter, in fact protect the territorial integrity of the member states of the United Nations organisation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But what is not clear to me is why this is being made into an issue since the final act of -- the Helsinki final act and the Paris Charter all confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I want to ask you about that. In a way, the Prosecutor brought into question the fact that the UN Charter protects, in a very direct way. the territorial integrity of its member states. But my question to you is whether you, as an expert --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Objection, objection that mischaracterised my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We are getting B/C/S on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry. Put what you actually said so that Mr. Perovic can see what you said and be able to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My questions were directed at page 5 of the report where it stated that the enactments of Croatia and Slovenia violated the UN Charter, and the reference was then made to, I believe, Article 2, section 4, which talks about international violations of territorial integrity, which would not apply since it is Croatia and Slovenia within the former Yugoslavia. That's what the discussion was about. But to say that we brought into question the fact that the UN Charter protects, in a very direct way, the territorial integrity of its member states is a complete mischaracterisation. It certainly does in Article 2, section 4, it does protect it from international encroachment, and my question was what the basis was for her assertion in her report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic? Any response to that objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure I understood what my learned colleague wanted to say. I remember quite clearly his questions relating to the Charter and his insisting on the expert witness pointing to the articles that directly protect the territorial integrity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe, Mr. Perovic, if you can point us in the transcript to the question exactly that you are referring to or the -- where you say he made the statement similar to what you have said, then he can be able to respond to that too. Just point us to yesterday's transcript, because I'm not able to remember the actual words used yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point, I cannot really quote you the relevant line, but it was one of the last questions during the third part of our session yesterday, just as our session drew to a close.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's of assistance, I did ask the witness to point to all the sections that refer to territorial integrity within the context of this question, though, but I never -- I never put that we, as described by Defence counsel. Nor would I, it's not our view. And I'm not sure why it's necessary to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic says it was towards the end of the cross-examination yesterday, and I'm trying to -- are you able to get to yesterday's transcript, Mr. Perovic, and look for it? It ended at page 11114. Actually, 11114 was -- we were giving an oral order at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order to avoid this whole confusion, I will rephrase my question. I can ask it in a different way and not even challenge what the Prosecutor said yesterday, not even bring it into any question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you wanted to do that, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Madam Avramov, among other things, the UN Charter was touched upon and the way in which it actually protects the territorial integrity of the member states of the United Nations organisation. My question to you in this regard is the following: Do you, as an expert, know of the existence of a single international instrument that would advocate the territorial disintegration of member states of the UN or subjects under international law; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is no such document, and I have to admit to you that I was quite flabbergasted by the question that was put to me yesterday regarding the UN Charter and the protection of the territorial integrity, because I assume that my learned colleagues have read, have studied, the statements of reason that are appended to the UN Charter to each of its articles when it was adopted, and the same principle was reiterated in the Helsinki final act and then in the Paris Charter. So this is something that is totally indisputable.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Avramov. I no further questions. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to thank you. Our expert witness wanted to say something, if you will allow her?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very briefly, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly. I just wanted to make a quick correction. I was asked yesterday when I published the first article on the Tribunal. I could not remember at the time, and then I went through my notes and it was in May, 1994. It was published in the journal of the Belgrade Law School. There is an abstract in English which is quite extensive, so I will leave it here with you so that you can see the first views of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said more about this point in my 1997 book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's been translated and you have it here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have completed my re-examination. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. Judge Hoepfel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No, thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge Nosworthy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ma'am we want to thank you very much for taking time from your very obviously busy schedule. You are now excused and you may now stand down. Once again, thank you very much. Thank you, ma'am. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with the completion of the examination of Professor Avramov, we've actually completed our working day today. Our next witness, ex-military expert Mr. Sekulic, arrived only today. We didn't have a chance to even talk to him. So we would like to start our examination tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will finish with him by the 20th or earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And since now I have the floor, I just wanted to ask to -- or to raise two issues. The first issue is the following: We should bear in mind that the site visit report has not yet been put on the record, and I just wanted to remind you it hasn't yet been admitted into evidence, because of the deadlines that we have ahead of us. And the second issue is the motion that we filed with regard to the filing of the Parker Commission report, in light of all the deadlines that we have ahead of us and all the tasks that we have to complete by those deadlines, just to bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just see what you're saying about the Parker Commission. The motion you filed in connection with the Parker Commission report, did you file it with this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour. We filed it on Monday, to the Trial Chamber, and I merely wanted to remind you, apologising for doing so, but we are doing it because of the deadlines that we have, so that this whole issue can be resolved before the end of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we filed our response to the motion this morning. We received the motion on Monday. We filed our response to it this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Parker Commission report?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. It's a motion for access to certain statements given to the Parker Commission into the death of Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those statements given by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By witnesses concerning the death. It's all set forth in the motion from the Defence and our response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will see it when we see it. I haven't seen the motion yet. I haven't seen your response either. Anyway, thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic, for mentioning those points. At least the point of the site report, the Chamber hadn't forgotten that. The site report is still being worked upon. We are waiting for the complete report to be finalized, and that will be placed on record as soon as it is finalised. Thank you very much. As regards the Parker Commission, as I've just said, I have -- I'm hearing of it for the first time today. I haven't seen your motion. I haven't seen the response by the Prosecution. But I would imagine that it will definitely be attended to in due course. Okay? Thank you very much. Having answered those, let me just then deal with the motion by the Defence on the request for leave for certification on the expert report of Mr. Sekulic. Again, it's going to be an oral decision because of the urgency of the matter. The Trial Chamber is seized of a Defence request filed today requesting the Trial Chamber to certify an interlocutory appeal of its decision concerning the expert Milislav Sekulic, dated the 13th of November 2006. The Trial Chamber notes the arguments of the Defence in the motion. The Trial Chamber also notes the arguments of the Prosecution as filed today. Under Rule 73(B) the Trial Chamber has first to decide whether the redaction of the expert report involves an issue which would significantly affect the fair and expeditious conduct of the proceedings or the outcome of the trial. Secondly, but only after having found that the first prong of the rule has been met, the Trial Chamber has to determine that an immediate resolution of that issue by the Appeals Chamber may materially advance the proceedings. The Trial Chamber finds that the first prong of the rule has not been met, and even if the Trial Chamber would have found that the first prong of the rule had been met, the Trial Chamber would not have granted leave for certification as the Trial Chamber finds, particularly in light of the late stage of the proceedings, that an immediate resolution by the Appeals Chamber would not materially advance the proceedings. In this regard, the Trial Chamber notes that the Defence was ordered to file this report immediately after the summer recess, that is on the 14th of August 2006. Thank you very much. Tomorrow is Thursday, the 16th. The Court will then stand adjourned until tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the same courtroom. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
